[T]he two approaches appear to converge in their fundamental 
analyses. Both approaches call for an assessment of the importance 
of the issue that Congress is delegating to an agency, as well as the 
bormdaries that Congress has imposed to cabin executive discretion. 
To be sure, the articulation of a standard—^“filling up the details”

of that standard. But the two approaches are not analytically 
different. They both require consideration of the same set of factors. 
Depending on the standard of review used in applying them, it may 
be that the daylight between these two articulations is marginal.

4. 
A Congressional Foilhack of Delegations? The Supreme Court is not 
the only institution that has been considering whether to rein in the delegation 
of power to agencies via substantive statutes. There are proposals for Congress 
to do finmAthing along the same lines, on a mass generic basis. Under the 
Regulations from the Executive in Need of Scrutiny (REINS) Act, passed by 
the Republican-controlled House of Representatives in each Congress from 
2011 to 2018 but never enacted, e.g., 115 H.R. 26, no “major” rule promulgated 
by any agency (with certain presidentially-authorized exceptions) would 
become effective unless and until Congress approved it by way of a joint 
resolution going through bicamerahsm and presentment. The REINS Act, if 
adopted, would effectively repeal the rulemaking powers of all agencies insofar 
as they might be exercised to adopt “major” rules.
5. 
Nondelegation's Connection to the Major Questions Doctrine. In 
Chapter 7, we will discuss the “major questions” doctrine (MQD), which, 
according to its most recent major formulation in West Virginia v. EP A, 597 
U.S. 697 (2022), requires a court to reject an interpretation of a substantive 
statute that would confer authority on an agency to decide a question of great 
economic or pohtical significance—^unless the statute clearly confers such 
authority. West Virginia says the MQD rests partly on “separation of powers 
principles” without saying exactly what those are. Id. at 723. As elaborated in 
Chapter 7, Justice Gorsuch claims the MQD derives from the nondelegation 
doctrine, but Justice Barrett has expressly rejected this idea, and some other 
Justices (including Roberts and Kavanaugh) have not weighed in on the MQD’s 
exact basis.
